# Understanding `@extends` vs `@include` in Laravel Views

When you are building a Laravel application, you will quickly find that view rendering is one of the most common points of confusion for developers coming from other frameworks or standard PHP. A frequent question arises regarding the difference between `@extends('layouts.masters.main')` and `@include('layouts.masters.main')`. While both directives ultimately merge content into a single output, they serve distinct architectural purposes within Laravel's Blade templating engine.

The primary distinction lies in the concept of inheritance versus composition. `@extends` establishes an inheritance relationship between a parent view and a child view. When you use `@extends('layouts.masters.main')`, you are telling Blade that the current file is a child template that relies on a specific parent layout to define its structure. This implies that the file containing the directive is not meant to be rendered in isolation; it expects a corresponding `@section` block defined later in the code to inject content into placeholders defined in the parent.

Consider a typical scenario where you have a base layout file named `layouts.masters.main`. This file likely contains your `<head>`, navigation bar, and footer. It defines sections like `@yield('content')` or `@stack('scripts')`. When you create a new view, such as `welcome.blade.php`, and start it with `@extends('layouts.masters.main')`, Blade expects this file to contain content within the yield blocks defined in the parent. The rendering process works by first loading the child view, then injecting its content into the parent's sections, and finally outputting the combined result. If you omit the `@section` definitions in the child view for a layout that uses `@yield`, Blade will throw an exception or skip rendering the yield blocks, which is often not the desired behavior.

In contrast, `@include('layouts.masters.main')` represents composition. It simply loads the specified file and inserts its raw content at the exact location of the directive within the current view. There is no expectation of matching sections or yields. If your parent layout uses `@yield('content')`, using `@include` will result in that yield block being skipped entirely because the included file is treated as a standalone snippet rather than a child template inheriting from the layout.

The reason tutorials and best practices strongly favor `@extends` for main application pages is that it enforces a separation of concerns between structure and content. Using `@include` for your entire page layout effectively duplicates the header and footer logic inside every single view file or relies on an inconsistent pattern where you forget to close sections. This leads to brittle codebases where changing a navigation menu requires editing dozens of files instead of just updating the parent layout.

However, there are valid use cases for `@include`. If you want to dynamically include a specific component, such as a sidebar or a modal dialog, within an existing page layout without creating a new child template relationship, `@include` is the correct tool. It allows you to compose views from smaller, reusable pieces without the strict contract of inheritance.

When deciding which directive to use, ask yourself if the file you are writing is meant to be a complete page that needs a header and footer defined elsewhere. If yes, it must be a child template using `@extends`. If you are merely inserting a specific UI element or including a partial within a larger context, `@include` is appropriate. Mixing these concepts often leads to "broken" layouts where the main content area does not appear because the yield block was skipped.
